# Your First Table {#chp:start}

A table is the one data visualization that everyone can read without a legend.
This chapter shows how to make one with **lt**, and then how to give it a title,
sensible labels, and a bit of polish.

## One function, many verbs {#sec:verbs}

Everything starts with `lt()`, which takes a data frame:

```{r}
library(lt)
lt(head(mtcars))
```

That is already a respectable table: numbers are rounded sensibly and right
aligned, and the column names are cleaned up. But the real fun begins when you
pipe it into one of the `lt_*()` verbs. Each verb adds one instruction to the
table, and you can stack as many as you like, in any order:

```{r}
lt(head(mtcars[, 1:4])) |>
  lt_header("Cars, Briefly", "Four measurements of six cars") |>
  lt_format(~ disp, decimals = 0) |>
  lt_note("Data from the 1974 Motor Trend US magazine.")
```

Notice that your data frame is never modified. A table is the data *plus* a
to-do list; the to-do list is carried out later, in the browser. That is why an
**lt** table can show `160` while remembering that the real value was `160.0`
(hover over a cell, or press <kbd>Alt</kbd> and click the table to reveal the
raw values).

The verbs fall into a few families (@tab:verb-families), which also happen to be
the chapters of this book.

:::: {.table #tab:verb-families}
::: caption
[ ](#@tab:verb-families) The verb families and where each is covered.
:::

| Family | Verbs |
|:-----------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------|
| Format values | `lt_format()`, `lt_date()`, `lt_sub()` (@chp:format) |
| Shape the table | `lt_spanner()`, `lt_merge()`, `lt_move()`, `lt_hide()`, `lt_group()`, `lt_indent()` (@chp:structure) |
| Explain it | `lt_footnote()`, `lt_note()`, `lt_html()` (@chp:notes) |
| Draw in cells | `lt_errorbar()`, `lt_sparkline()`, `lt_dotplot()` (@chp:plots) |
| Style it | `lt_style()`, `lt_css()`, `lt_wrap()` (@chp:style) |
| Make it interactive | `lt_interactive()`, `lt_viewer()`, `lt_serve()` (@chp:interactive) |
| Shiny | `lt_output()`, `render_lt()`, `lt_input()` (@chp:shiny) |
| Get it out | `lt_export()`, `lt_spec()` (@chp:export) |
::::

Many verbs take columns as their second argument. You can name them as a
one-sided formula (`~ mpg + disp`), as a character vector (`c("mpg", "disp")`),
or by position (`1:2`). A formula can even use the pronoun `.` for "the column
names", so `~ endsWith(., "_time")` selects every column whose name ends in
`_time`.

## The cheat sheet {#sec:cheatsheet}

Before we go through the verbs one by one, here is the whole package on one
page. This table is self-documenting: each function's name is placed exactly
where that function acts. The title reads `lt_header(title = ...)` because
`lt_header()` put it there; each column header is the name of the function that
shaped the column; the row group label is `lt_group()`; and the footnotes
explain the rest. Come back to it whenever you want a quick reminder, and
perhaps try to guess which verb is responsible for each detail before reading on.

```{r, child = ex('lt')}
```

## Titles and labels {#sec:labels}

`lt_header()` puts a title, and optionally a subtitle, above the table:

```{r, child = ex('header')}
```

Column names are cleaned for display: dots and underscores become spaces, so
`Sepal.Length` is shown as "Sepal Length". Use `auto_label = FALSE` if you want
the raw names back, or `lt_label()` to say exactly what a column should be
called. `lt_label()` also accepts a named list or vector if your labels are
already stored somewhere:

```{r, child = ex('label')}
```

A label does not have to be plain text. Wrap it in `I()` to use HTML, as shown
in @sec:html.

## Alignment and widths {#sec:align}

Numbers are right-aligned and text is left-aligned, which is what you want most
of the time. When it is not, `lt_align()` takes `"left"`, `"center"`, or
`"right"`, and `lt_width()` sets how wide a column is, in any CSS unit. Call
`lt_width()` with an unnamed argument to set the width of the whole table:

```{r, child = ex('align-width')}
```

## What kind of column is this? {#sec:types}

When you explore a new data set, the first question is often "what *is* this
column?". With `show_types = TRUE`, `lt()` tags each column with its type, the
same way a tibble does when printed: `<dbl>`, `<chr>`, `<fct>`, `<date>`, and
so on. It also makes a pleasant default for tables meant for exploration (see
`lt_viewer()` in @sec:viewer).

```{r, child = ex('show-types')}
```

## Where tables show up {#sec:printing}

An `lt` table is displayed wherever R can display HTML:

-   **At the console**, printing a table opens it in the RStudio or Positron
    viewer, or in your web browser otherwise. The table is scaled to fit the
    window, and a table that is too tall scrolls inside its frame with the
    header kept in view.

-   **In a document**, you simply print it, from a chunk of a
    [litedown](https://yihui.org/litedown/) document, a **knitr** R Markdown
    document, or a Quarto document. The runtime assets are included once per
    page, however many tables the page holds. In a `litedown::fuse()` document,
    tables built from the same data frame also share one copy of the data, which
    keeps the output file small.

-   **In a Shiny app**, with `lt_output()` and `render_lt()` (@chp:shiny).

-   **In a file**, with `lt_export()`: standalone HTML, PDF, or PNG
    (@chp:export).

Because a table is just an object until it is printed, you can build it in a
function, return it from a package, and let the caller add a few verbs of their
own. That is how a package can offer tables that its users can still customize
(@chp:extend).

By default, `NA` is displayed as an em dash (—), so that a missing value is never
mistaken for an empty string. To show something else everywhere, set
`options(lt.missing = "n/a")`; to leave `NA` cells blank, use `""`. To change it
for one column, use `lt_sub()` (@sec:sub).
